prompt.en: A weekly net keeps the same UTC schedule. Your local clock offset changes for the season. How should you update a local calendar reminder?

text.en: Keep local time fixed by moving the published UTC event time.

feedback.en: That changes the event instead of converting its time. A fixed UTC schedule may have a different local time.

text.en: Recalculate local time using the offset on the event date, keeping UTC fixed.

feedback.en: Use the event-date offset and check for a date crossing. UTC stays the shared schedule.

text.en: Keep the earlier local reminder until the net changes its UTC schedule.

feedback.en: The local offset changed even though the UTC event did not. The old reminder can now be an hour off.

text.en: Use the offset on the date you entered the reminder, rather than the event date.

feedback.en: The relevant offset is the one in force when the event occurs. Entry time does not set the conversion.

explanation.en: A fixed UTC schedule can move on the local clock when the offset changes. Convert using the offset on the event date.

prompt.en: A club gives you an azimuthal map centred far from your home station. You want a bearing from home to a distant contact. Which method is suitable?

text.en: Use the club map bearing because the destination is unchanged.

feedback.en: A bearing depends on the starting point as well as the destination. The club centre is a different starting point.

text.en: Use the reciprocal of the club bearing because your station is at a different centre.

feedback.en: A reciprocal reverses a path from the same starting point. It does not move the map centre to your station.

text.en: Use an azimuthal map centred on your home station.

feedback.en: A home-centred map gives outward bearings from your own location to the destination.

text.en: Use the club bearing after adjusting it by your UTC offset.

feedback.en: Time-zone conversion changes clock labels, not the map geometry between stations.

explanation.en: Azimuthal bearings radiate from the map centre. Use your own station as that centre for home antenna headings.

prompt.en: Your log shows better reception just after you turn the antenna. The distant station kept the same power. What would best test whether antenna direction caused the improvement?

text.en: Compare repeated turns between the headings while watching for path changes.

feedback.en: Repeated comparisons with other settings held steady give better evidence than one change. Propagation can still vary, so watch the path.

text.en: Treat the time order in the log as sufficient proof of the cause.

feedback.en: The log shows sequence, not control over other causes. A path change could have happened at the same time.

text.en: Treat unchanged transmitter power as proof that propagation stayed fixed.

feedback.en: Transmitter power and propagation are different conditions. One can stay fixed while the other changes.

text.en: Compare a later reading using a different receiver gain setting.

feedback.en: Changing receiver gain adds another cause for a meter difference. Hold settings steady to compare antenna headings.

explanation.en: A log preserves observations. Repeated comparisons with other conditions held steady help distinguish an antenna effect from changing propagation.
